intro: Muslims believe the Qur'an came to one man, Muhammad, over about 23 years. Those years had a shape. First there were quiet years in a trade city called Mecca. Then came hard years, when the city's leaders pushed back. Then a move to a new town, Medina, where a small group became a community with rules, battles, treaties and, at last, a book.

This unit tells that story as Muslims tell it, with the dates marked "about," and with notes on what historians can and cannot check. The Prophet's life is not the Qur'an. But Muslims read the two together. A verse about orphans sounds different when you know the Prophet was one. A verse about peace sounds different when you know a treaty had just been signed.

By the end, you will be able to put the main events in order, name the first Muslims and the two cities, explain what the hijra is and why Muslim years count from it, and tell how, according to tradition, spoken words became a written book.
bigQuestion: How does knowing the story of Muhammad's life help a reader understand the Qur'an?

timeline.t: Muhammad is born in Mecca, as Muslim tradition tells it
In the cave of Hira, Muslims believe, the first words of the Qur'an come
Muhammad begins to teach in public; Quraysh leaders grow angry
Some Muslims go to Abyssinia, where a Christian king protects them

The Year of Sorrow: Khadijah and Abu Talib die
The hijra: the Muslims move to Yathrib, later called Medina
Battle of Badr; the qibla turns toward Mecca
Battle of the Trench saves Medina
Treaty of Hudaybiyyah brings peace with Quraysh
Muhammad returns to Mecca; the idols leave the Kaaba
Farewell Pilgrimage; Muhammad dies in Medina

the square stone building in Mecca that Muslims believe was first built for the one God
a message that believers say came from God
the Muslim belief that there is only one God
the leading tribe of Mecca, into which Muhammad was born
when a group refuses to trade or deal with someone, to force a change
the move of Muhammad and the Muslims from Mecca to Medina in 622
a building where Muslims gather to pray
the people of Medina who helped and took in the Muslims from Mecca
the direction Muslims face when they pray, toward the Kaaba in Mecca
a written peace agreement between two sides
the leader of the Muslim community after Muhammad; the word means one who comes after

A farming town with many wells
test.why: Mecca was a caravan trade city, and its Kaaba held many idols.

test.q: Who does tradition say brought the first words of the Qur'an to Muhammad?
test.why: Muslims believe the angel Jibril (Gabriel) came to Muhammad in the cave of Hira.
Tawhid is the belief in one God, the heart of the Qur'an's message.

test.q: Which of these was among the first Muslims, as tradition tells it?
test.why: Bilal, an enslaved man from Abyssinia, was one of the first Muslims.

test.q: Why did Quraysh leaders oppose the message?
choices: The idols brought money, and the message said the rich would be judged too
They wanted to move to Medina
test.why: The idols drew visitors and wealth. The message put rich and poor on the same footing before God.

choices: Let them stay and protected them
test.why: Tradition says the king heard Surah Maryam recited and refused to send the Muslims back.

choices: A speech at the end of a pilgrimage
The move from Mecca to Medina in 622
test.why: The hijra is the move of the Muslims from Mecca to Medina in 622.

test.q: The Muslim calendar counts years from which event?
test.why: Hijri years, marked AH, begin with the hijra in 622.

choices: The people of Medina who helped the Muslims from Mecca
The scribes who wrote the Qur'an
test.why: Ansar means helpers. They were the people of Medina who took in the newcomers.

choices: The direction Muslims face to pray
A share given to the poor
test.why: The qibla is the direction of prayer. In about 624 it became the Kaaba in Mecca.

test.q: Which battle did the Muslims win in 624?
test.why: At Badr in 624 the smaller Muslim force beat an army from Quraysh.

choices: A plan to dig a trench
A peace deal with Quraysh in 628
test.why: In 628 the Muslims and Quraysh signed a peace treaty at Hudaybiyyah.

test.why: When Mecca gave in, Muhammad had the idols removed so the Kaaba was for one God.

test.q: What does the Farewell Sermon say makes a person better?
test.why: Tradition says the sermon taught that only good deeds, not tribe or color, make one person better.

test.q: How do Muslims say the Qur'an became one book?
choices: Muhammad wrote it himself in Mecca
The king of Abyssinia printed it
It was gathered after Muhammad's death and a standard copy was made under Uthman
Each tribe kept its own book
test.why: Tradition says Abu Bakr had it gathered and Uthman had a standard copy made in about 650.

write.prompt: The Qur'an says not to push away the orphan (93:9–10), and it says God made people into nations and tribes so they could know one another (49:13). Pick one of these passages. Tell what it says. Then explain how one event from Muhammad's life, as Muslims tell it, helps a reader understand it.
tips: Name the surah and ayah you are writing about.
Say "Muslims believe" or "tradition says" when you tell what people believe.
Pick one event from Mecca or Medina and tell it in order.
Use words from this unit, like revelation, hijra or qibla.
Describe, do not judge. Your job is to explain, not to say who is right.

title: The Life of the Prophet as Context

chapters.title: Mecca: The Message and the Hard Years
chapters.bigQuestion: What did the first Muslims in Mecca hear, and why was it hard for them to stay?

story.title: A Voice from the Rooftop
story.kicker: A man who was once enslaved climbs up high and calls his friends to prayer.
paragraphs: It is early morning in Medina. The sky is still gray. A tall man named Bilal climbs onto the flat roof of a house. He takes a deep breath. Then he calls out in a strong, clear voice. Muslim tradition says this was the first call to prayer, the adhan. People stop what they are doing and listen.

Bilal had come a long way to reach that rooftop. Years before, in the city of Mecca, he was enslaved. He heard Muhammad teach that there is only one God. Bilal believed it. His owner was angry and punished him under the hot sun. Tradition says Bilal kept saying one word: "Ahad," which means "One."

A friend of Muhammad named Abu Bakr paid to set Bilal free. After that, Bilal stayed close to Muhammad. He was one of the first Muslims. Many of them had hard years in Mecca. Some were poor. Some were enslaved. The leaders of the city did not want their new message.

This chapter goes back to those years in Mecca. It tells how Muslims say the message began, what it said, and why the city pushed back. Muslims tell this story with love. Historians study it carefully. We will listen to both. And we will keep hearing Bilal's voice, high on that roof.
story.think: Why do you think Muslim tradition remembers Bilal so well, when he began as an enslaved man with no power?

lessons.title: Tribes and Camel Roads
lessons.mainIdea: Before Islam, Arabia was a land of tribes, and Mecca was a busy trade city on the camel roads.
reading: Arabia is a big, dry land. About 1,400 years ago, most people there lived in a *tribe*. A tribe is a large family group. Your tribe kept you safe. If you had no tribe, you had no one to protect you. Tribes made deals with each other, and sometimes they fought.

Some tribes moved from place to place with their camels and sheep. Others lived in towns. Mecca was a town in a rocky valley. It had a well called Zamzam. Camel caravans stopped there to rest and trade. A *caravan* is a long line of camels carrying goods. Caravans carried spices, cloth and leather.

The strongest tribe in Mecca was called Quraysh. They ran the trade and took care of the town's holy place. Muhammad was born into this tribe. Historians know these things from old poems, from later Muslim writers, and from what other lands wrote about Arabia.

words.d: a large family group that lives and travels together and protects its members
a long line of camels and people carrying goods to sell in another place

look.title: Picture the Caravan
look.text: Picture a line of forty camels walking into Mecca at sunset. Bells ring on their necks. Each camel carries heavy bags. The drivers are tired and dusty. At the town well, boys run up to bring water. Merchants come out to ask what the camels carry and what it will cost.
look.prompt: What might a boy who lived in Mecca learn just from watching caravans come and go?

check.q: What was a tribe in old Arabia?
choices: A large family group that protected its members
check.why: A tribe was a big family group. It kept its members safe.

check.q: What is a caravan?
choices: A line of camels carrying goods
check.why: A caravan is a line of camels and people carrying goods to trade.

check.q: Which tribe ran Mecca's trade and holy place?
check.why: Quraysh was the strong tribe of Mecca. Muhammad was born into it.

lessons.title: The Kaaba and Many Gods
lessons.mainIdea: Mecca's holy place, the Kaaba, was full of idols before Islam, and people came from far away to visit it.
reading: In the middle of Mecca stood a square stone building called the *Kaaba*. It was old even then. Arab tribes believed it was a house for the gods. Muslim tradition says Ibrahim (Abraham) and his son Ismail (Ishmael) first built it for the one God, and that people forgot.

By Muhammad's time, the Kaaba held many idols. An *idol* is a statue that people pray to. Tradition says there were hundreds. Each tribe had its own gods. Some people in Arabia were Jews or Christians and prayed to one God. Most people in Mecca prayed to many.

Every year, tribes came to Mecca to visit the Kaaba. They walked around it. They also bought and sold goods. This made Quraysh rich. Later, the Qur'an would say that the Kaaba should be for one God only. That idea would change the whole city.

words.d: the square stone building in Mecca that Muslims believe was first built for the one God
a statue or image that people pray to as a god

look.title: How Far the Caravans Went
look.cite: Rounded straight-line distances from modern maps
look.prompt: A camel walks about 40 kilometers a day. About how many days was the trip from Mecca to Yathrib?

check.q: What is an idol?
check.why: An idol is a statue or image that people pray to as a god.

check.q: Who do Muslims believe first built the Kaaba?
check.why: Muslim tradition says Ibrahim (Abraham) and Ismail (Ishmael) built the Kaaba for one God.

check.q: Before Islam, most people in Mecca prayed to
check.why: Most people in Mecca prayed to many gods and idols. Some Jews and Christians in Arabia prayed to one God.

lessons.title: A Boy Called Trustworthy
lessons.mainIdea: Muslim tradition tells of Muhammad's early life in Mecca: an orphan, a shepherd, a trader people trusted, and a man who went to a cave to think.
reading: Muslim tradition says Muhammad was born in Mecca in about the year 570. His father died before he was born. His mother died when he was small. His grandfather cared for him, and then his uncle Abu Talib did. As a boy he watched sheep and camels.

When he grew up, Muhammad traded goods for a rich woman named Khadijah. She saw that he was honest. People in Mecca called him al-Amin, "the trustworthy." Khadijah asked him to marry her. Tradition says he was about 25 and she was about 40. They had children together.

Muhammad did not like the idols or the greed of the city. He liked to walk to a cave on a mountain near Mecca. The cave is called Hira. There he sat alone and thought. Historians cannot check most of these early stories. But this is how Muslims have told them for a very long time.

words.d: a child whose mother or father has died
a story or a way of doing things that a group passes down over many years
the cave on a mountain near Mecca where Muslims say Muhammad went to think

look.title: Two Ways to Tell It
look.text: A Muslim writer says: "Muhammad was born in the Year of the Elephant, and his mother saw a light when he was born." A historian says: "Muhammad was born in Mecca in about 570. Early sources are later than his life, so exact details are hard to check." Both are talking about the same person.
look.prompt: How are these two ways of telling the story different? What is each writer trying to do?

check.q: About when do Muslims say Muhammad was born?
check.why: Tradition places his birth in Mecca in about the year 570.

check.q: What did people in Mecca call Muhammad?
check.why: He was called al-Amin, "the trustworthy," because he was honest in trade.

check.q: Who was Khadijah?
choices: A leader of Quraysh who opposed him
check.why: Khadijah was a wealthy trader. She married Muhammad and was the first to believe his message.

lessons.title: Read!
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims believe that in about 610, in the cave of Hira, the angel Jibril brought Muhammad the first words of the Qur'an.
reading: Muslim tradition tells it this way. Muhammad was about 40 years old. He was alone in the cave of Hira. Suddenly an *angel* was there. Muslims name him Jibril (Gabriel). The angel said, "Read!" Muhammad answered that he could not read. The angel held him tight and said it again.

Then, Muslims believe, the first words of the *Qur'an* came. They are in Surah 96, called Al-'Alaq. In simple words they say: Read, in the name of your Lord who made people. Your Lord taught by the pen. He taught people what they did not know. This was in about the year 610.

Muhammad was afraid. He ran home to Khadijah and asked her to cover him. She calmed him. She believed him. Muslims call this the first *revelation*. A revelation is a message that Muslims believe came from God. More messages came for the next 23 years.

words.d: a messenger from God, in the beliefs of Muslims, Jews and Christians
the holy book of Islam; Muslims believe its words came from God through Muhammad
a message that believers say came from God

look.title: The First Five Ayahs
look.text: In simple words, the surah begins: Read, in the name of your Lord who created. He created a human being from a tiny clinging thing. Read, for your Lord is most generous. He taught by the pen. He taught people what they did not know.
look.cite: Qur'an 96:1–5 (Al-'Alaq), paraphrased from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: The first word is "Read." Why might that word matter so much to Muslims?

check.q: What was the first word the angel said, as Muslims tell it?
check.why: The angel said "Read!" (Iqra). The first ayahs of Surah 96 begin with that word.

check.q: Who calmed Muhammad after the cave?
check.why: He ran home to his wife Khadijah, who covered him and believed him.

check.q: What is a revelation, in this lesson?
choices: A message believers say came from God
check.why: Muslims call the Qur'an's words revelations, messages they believe God sent.

lessons.title: One God, and Be Fair
lessons.mainIdea: The early Meccan surahs teach that there is one God and that people must be fair and care for orphans and the poor.
reading: The first messages were short. Muslims say they came bit by bit over many years. Their biggest idea was this: there is only one God. Muslims call this *tawhid*. The idols in the Kaaba were nothing. This was a shock in a city full of idols.

The messages also said that people would answer to God for how they lived. They spoke about the *Day of Judgment*. On that day, Muslims believe, every person's good and bad deeds are weighed. The rich could not buy their way out. This was a big idea for the poor of Mecca.

The Qur'an told Mecca to be fair. Surah 93 says not to push away the orphan. It says not to turn away a person who asks for help. Surah 107 says a person who pushes away the orphan does not really believe. The early Muslims heard this as a call to be kind and honest.

words.d: the Muslim belief that there is only one God
the day when, Muslims believe, God will judge every person's deeds

look.title: Do Not Push Away the Orphan
look.text: In simple words, the surah says: Your Lord did not leave you and does not hate you. Did he not find you an orphan and give you a home? So do not treat the orphan harshly. Do not turn away the one who asks for help. And tell about the good your Lord has done.
look.cite: Qur'an 93:3, 6, 9–11 (Ad-Duha), paraphrased from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: Muhammad was an orphan himself. How might that change the way he heard these words?

check.q: What does tawhid mean?
check.why: Tawhid is the belief in one God. It was the first message's biggest idea.

check.q: What does Surah 93 tell people about orphans?
check.why: Surah 93 says not to push away or treat the orphan harshly.

check.q: Why was the Day of Judgment a big idea for poor people in Mecca?
choices: It said the rich could not buy their way out
check.why: The Qur'an says deeds are weighed, not money. That gave the poor equal standing.

lessons.title: The First Muslims
lessons.mainIdea: Muslim tradition names the first believers: Khadijah, the boy Ali, the friend Abu Bakr, and Bilal, who was enslaved.
reading: Muslims call a person who accepts the message a *Muslim*. The word means "one who gives in to God." Tradition says the very first Muslim was Khadijah, Muhammad's wife. Next came Ali, his young cousin, who lived in his house. Ali was about ten years old.

A friend named Abu Bakr believed next. He was a trader, calm and kind. He told his friends about the message. Abu Bakr later used his money to buy enslaved people who had become Muslims and set them free. One of them was Bilal.

Bilal came from Abyssinia, in Africa. His owner hurt him for believing in one God. Tradition says he would not give up. Abu Bakr freed him. A man named Zayd, whom Muhammad had adopted, believed too. The first Muslims were a small, mixed group: rich and poor, old and young, free and enslaved.

words.d: a person who follows Islam; the word means one who gives in to God
forced to work for an owner as property, without freedom

look.title: Ages When the Message Began
look.cite: Ages as given in Muslim tradition (the sira); historians treat them as approximate
look.prompt: The first Muslims were very different ages. Why might that matter for a new group?

check.q: Who does tradition name as the very first Muslim?
check.why: Muslim tradition says Khadijah, Muhammad's wife, was the first to believe.

check.q: What did Abu Bakr do for Bilal?
check.why: Abu Bakr bought Bilal from his owner and freed him.

check.q: What does the word Muslim mean?
choices: One who gives in to God
check.why: Muslim means one who submits, or gives in, to God.

lessons.title: Mecca's Leaders Say No
lessons.mainIdea: When Muhammad began to teach in public, the leaders of Quraysh grew angry and made life hard for the Muslims.
reading: For about three years, tradition says, the message stayed among family and friends. Then, in about 613, Muhammad began to teach in the open. He stood near the Kaaba and told Mecca to leave its idols. Most people laughed. Some got angry.

The leaders of Quraysh had reasons to be angry. The idols brought visitors and money to Mecca. The message said the rich would be judged like everyone else. And it came from a man they knew, not a king. One of Muhammad's own uncles, Abu Lahab, became his enemy.

The leaders could not hurt Muhammad much, because his uncle Abu Talib protected him. But they could hurt Muslims with no tribe to protect them. Enslaved Muslims like Bilal were punished. A woman named Sumayya was killed. Tradition remembers her as the first Muslim to die for the faith.

words.d: the leading tribe of Mecca, which ran the city's trade and the Kaaba
to treat people cruelly because of what they believe

look.title: Why Were They Angry?
look.text: Imagine you run a shop next to a famous statue. People come from far away to see the statue, and they buy from your shop. Then a neighbor starts telling everyone that the statue is nothing and should be taken down. He also says you have been unfair to poor people.
look.prompt: Why might the shop owner be angry? Which reason is about money, and which is about pride?

check.q: In about what year did Muhammad begin teaching in public?
check.why: Tradition says the message stayed private for about three years, then went public in about 613.

check.q: Why could the leaders of Quraysh not easily hurt Muhammad himself?
choices: His uncle Abu Talib protected him
check.why: Abu Talib was a leader in his clan and kept Muhammad under his protection.

check.q: Who does tradition remember as the first Muslim to die for the faith?
check.why: Sumayya, an enslaved woman, was killed for believing. Tradition honors her as the first martyr.

lessons.title: Safe with a Christian King
lessons.mainIdea: Muslim tradition says some early Muslims went to Abyssinia, where a Christian king heard the Qur'an and protected them.
reading: In about 615, tradition says, Muhammad told some Muslims to leave Mecca for a while. They crossed the Red Sea to *Abyssinia*, a land in Africa now called Ethiopia. Its king was a Christian. Muhammad had heard that he was fair to strangers.

The leaders of Quraysh sent men after them with gifts for the king. They asked him to send the Muslims back. The king called both sides in. A Muslim named Ja'far, Ali's older brother, spoke for his group. He recited part of Surah 19, called Maryam, about Mary and the birth of Isa (Jesus).

Tradition says the king wept when he heard it. He said the Muslims could stay. He would not send them back. Muslims remember this as a time when a Christian ruler kept them safe. Historians note that the story comes from later Muslim writers, but they agree Muslims did go to Abyssinia.

words.d: an old name for the land in Africa now called Ethiopia
to say a text aloud from memory, with care

look.title: In the King's Hall
look.text: Picture a wide hall with a stone floor. A king sits on a raised seat, with priests beside him. On one side stand men from Mecca holding gifts of leather. On the other stand tired travelers who just crossed the sea. One of them steps forward and begins to recite, slowly, a chapter about Maryam and her baby.
look.prompt: Why might Ja'far have chosen a surah about Maryam to recite to a Christian king?

check.q: Where did some early Muslims go to be safe?
check.why: They crossed the Red Sea to Abyssinia, now Ethiopia, in about 615.

check.q: What did Ja'far recite to the king?
check.why: Tradition says Ja'far recited from Surah Maryam, about Mary and the birth of Isa.

check.q: What did the king decide?
choices: To become a Muslim leader in Mecca
To send the gifts to Quraysh
check.why: The Christian king refused to send them back and let them stay in his land.

lessons.title: The Boycott and the Sad Year
lessons.mainIdea: Quraysh cut off Muhammad's clan for about three years, and soon after, Muhammad lost both Khadijah and Abu Talib.
reading: The leaders of Quraysh tried a new plan. In about 616 they made a rule: no one could trade with Muhammad's clan or marry into it. This is called a *boycott*. His clan, Banu Hashim, moved to a valley outside the town. Tradition says food was scarce for about three years.

The boycott ended in about 619. But that year brought more sadness. Khadijah died. She had believed in Muhammad first and stood by him for 25 years. Then his uncle Abu Talib died. Abu Talib had kept him safe. Muslims call this the Year of Sorrow.

Now no strong person in Mecca protected Muhammad. He went to the town of Ta'if to ask for help. Its leaders drove him out. Tradition says boys threw stones at him. He came back to Mecca sad but not ready to give up. The next years would bring a way out.

words.d: when a group refuses to buy from, sell to or deal with someone, to force a change
a smaller family group inside a tribe

look.title: The Meccan Years in Order
look.unit: year CE (about, as tradition tells it)
look.cite: Dates from Muslim tradition (the sira); historians mark them all as approximate
look.prompt: About how many years passed between the first words in the cave and the move to Yathrib?

check.q: What is a boycott?
choices: Refusing to trade or deal with a group
check.why: Quraysh refused to trade with or marry into Muhammad's clan. That is a boycott.

check.q: Which two people died in the Year of Sorrow?
check.why: Muhammad's wife Khadijah and his uncle Abu Talib both died in about 619.

check.q: What happened when Muhammad went to Ta'if?
choices: He met the king of Abyssinia
check.why: Ta'if's leaders refused to help him. Tradition says he was chased out with stones.

lessons.title: The Night Journey
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims tell of a night when Muhammad was carried to Jerusalem and up through the heavens, a story linked to Surah 17.
reading: Muslims tell a story from about the year 620. One night, they say, the angel Jibril woke Muhammad. A winged animal called Buraq carried him from Mecca to Jerusalem. Muslims call this the *Isra*, the night journey. In Jerusalem, tradition says, he prayed with earlier prophets.

Then, the story goes, Muhammad rose up through the heavens. Muslims call this the *Mi'raj*, the ascent. Tradition says he met prophets like Musa (Moses) and Isa (Jesus). He came before God. Muslims believe that on this night the five daily prayers were given to them.

The Qur'an speaks of the journey in one ayah, at the start of Surah 17. It praises God, who took his servant by night from the holy place in Mecca to the far-off holy place. Muslims read this as Jerusalem. Some Muslims say the journey was in the body; some say it was a vision. Both readings are old.

words.d: the night journey Muslims believe took Muhammad from Mecca to Jerusalem
the ascent Muslims believe took Muhammad up through the heavens

look.title: By Night to the Far Place
look.text: In simple words, the ayah says: Praise be to God, who carried his servant by night from the holy place of worship to the far-off place of worship, whose surroundings God blessed, to show him some of God's signs. God hears and sees everything.
look.cite: Qur'an 17:1 (Al-Isra), paraphrased from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: The ayah does not name Jerusalem. How do you think Muslims came to read it that way?

check.q: Where does Muslim tradition say the night journey went first?
check.why: The Isra, the night journey, took Muhammad from Mecca to Jerusalem, Muslims say.

check.q: What is the Mi'raj?
check.why: Mi'raj means the ascent. Muslims believe Muhammad rose through the heavens that night.

check.q: Which surah begins with the night journey?
check.why: Surah 17, Al-Isra, opens with the ayah about the journey by night.

review.q: What was the Kaaba like before Islam, as tradition tells it?
choices: Full of idols that many tribes visited
review.why: The Kaaba held many idols. Tribes came each year to visit it and to trade.

review.q: In about what year do Muslims say the first revelation came?
review.why: Tradition places the first words in the cave of Hira in about 610, when Muhammad was about 40.

review.q: Which idea was the center of the first message?
review.why: Tawhid, belief in one God, was the heart of the message.

review.q: Why did the leaders of Quraysh oppose Muhammad?
choices: The idols brought money, and the message judged the rich
review.why: The idols brought visitors and wealth. The message said all would be judged, rich and poor alike.

review.q: What did the Christian king of Abyssinia do?
choices: Sent the Muslims back to Mecca
Let the Muslims stay in his land
review.why: Tradition says the king heard Surah Maryam and refused to send the Muslims back.

choices: Quraysh refusing to trade with Muhammad's clan
review.why: For about three years, Quraysh cut off trade and marriage with Banu Hashim.

choices: An enslaved man who became one of the first Muslims and was freed
review.why: Bilal, from Abyssinia, was enslaved in Mecca, believed the message and was freed by Abu Bakr.

review.q: How does this course talk about the night journey?
choices: As a story Muslims tell and read in Surah 17
As a story from the Bible
review.why: We describe what Muslims believe and what the Qur'an says. We do not judge if it is true.

chapters.title: Medina: The Hijra and a Community
chapters.bigQuestion: How did a small group of Muslims from Mecca become a community with its own city, rules and book?

story.title: The City That Changed Its Name
story.kicker: A town called Yathrib takes in some tired travelers and gets a new name.
paragraphs: A town sat in a green valley about 340 kilometers north of Mecca. It had date palms, wells and farms. Its name was Yathrib. Two big Arab tribes lived there, and they had fought each other for years. Jewish tribes lived there too, farming and making things. The town needed peace.

Some men from Yathrib had met Muhammad in Mecca. They liked his message. They asked him to come and help their town. So in the year 622, small groups of Muslims began to slip out of Mecca. They walked or rode north through the desert. Muhammad came last, with Abu Bakr.

Tradition says that when he reached the edge of Yathrib, people ran out to meet him. Children sang. Everyone wanted him to stay at their house. He let his camel walk until it knelt down. That spot became his home and his mosque. It is still there today, much bigger, in the Prophet's Mosque.

Soon people stopped saying Yathrib. They called the town Madinat an-Nabi, "the City of the Prophet." We say Medina. For the next ten years, this city was the home of the Muslims. Here they made rules, fought battles, made peace, and heard the rest of the Qur'an.

This chapter follows those ten years. It tells them as Muslims tell them, and notes what historians say. Along the way, watch for how a group of friends becomes a community, and how a set of spoken words becomes a book.
story.think: What does it tell you about a town when its people rename it after one person who moved there?

lessons.title: An Invitation from the North
lessons.mainIdea: People from Yathrib met Muhammad in Mecca, made promises to protect him, and invited the Muslims to their town.
reading: Every year, people from all over Arabia came to Mecca to visit the Kaaba. Muhammad spoke to the visitors about one God. Most said no. But in about 620, a few men from Yathrib listened. They went home and told others. The next year, more came.

Yathrib was a farming town far to the north. Its two main Arab tribes had fought a long war. Many people there were tired of it. They wanted a fair person from outside to settle their fights. Some of them thought Muhammad could be that person.

In about 621 and again in 622, tradition says, groups from Yathrib met Muhammad at night near Mecca, at a place called Aqaba. They made a *pledge*, a serious promise. They promised to protect him as they would protect their own families. Now the Muslims had somewhere to go.

words.d: a serious promise to do something
the old name of the town that became Medina

look.title: A Promise in the Dark
look.text: Picture a night meeting on a hillside outside Mecca. About seventy people from Yathrib sit close together, keeping their voices low. They have traveled for two weeks. One by one they take Muhammad's hand and promise to protect him. They know that Quraysh would be angry if they found out.
look.prompt: Why do you think the meeting had to be secret? What were the people from Yathrib risking?

check.q: Why did some people in Yathrib want Muhammad to come?
choices: Their tribes had fought a long war and wanted a fair judge
check.why: Yathrib's tribes were tired of fighting. They wanted a fair outsider to settle their disputes.

check.q: What is a pledge?
check.why: The people of Yathrib made a pledge, a serious promise, to protect Muhammad.

check.q: Where did the night meetings with Muhammad happen?
check.why: Tradition calls them the pledges of Aqaba, after the place near Mecca where they met.

lessons.title: The Hijra
lessons.mainIdea: In 622 the Muslims moved from Mecca to Yathrib; Muslims call this the hijra, and their calendar counts years from it.
reading: The move from Mecca to Yathrib is called the *hijra*. The word means "leaving" or "moving away." Muslims left in small groups. They did not want Quraysh to notice. Tradition says Quraysh leaders planned to kill Muhammad before he could go. Ali slept in his bed so they would think he was home.

Muhammad and Abu Bakr slipped out and hid in a cave on a mountain called Thawr. Tradition tells that a spider spun a web across the cave's mouth. The men hunting them saw the web and did not look inside. After three days, the two friends rode north. The trip took about ten days.

The hijra happened in the year 622. It was such a big change that Muslims count years from it. Their *calendar* is called the Hijri calendar. Its years are marked AH. Muslim tradition says the second caliph, Umar, set the calendar this way some years after the Prophet died. Hijri years follow the moon, so they are a little shorter than ours.

words.d: the move of Muhammad and the Muslims from Mecca to Medina in 622
a way of counting days, months and years
the label for years in the Muslim calendar, counted from the hijra

look.title: Hijri Years and Our Years
look.cite: Standard Hijri to Gregorian conversion; a Hijri year is about 11 days shorter than a solar year
look.prompt: Look at the gaps. Why does year 1000 AH not land on the year 1622?

check.q: What does hijra mean?
check.why: Hijra means moving away. It names the Muslims' move from Mecca to Medina.

check.q: In what year was the hijra?
check.why: The hijra took place in 622 CE. Muslim years are counted from it.

check.q: What do the letters AH mark?
check.why: AH labels Hijri years, counted from the hijra in 622.

lessons.title: A Mosque and New Brothers
lessons.mainIdea: In Medina the Muslims built a simple mosque, and the people who moved and the people who helped them became one community.
reading: The first thing the Muslims built was a *mosque*, a place for prayer. Tradition says Muhammad stopped first at a village called Quba and built a small mosque there. In Yathrib itself he built one where his camel had knelt. It had mud walls and a roof of palm branches.

The mosque was not only for prayer. People met there, ate there and settled fights there. Muhammad's own rooms were beside it. Poor Muslims with no home slept on a bench along one wall. Muslims believe this simple building was the model for every mosque after it.

The Muslims who moved from Mecca were called the *Muhajirun*. The word means "the ones who moved." The people of Yathrib who helped them were the *Ansar*, "the helpers." Tradition says Muhammad paired each newcomer with a helper. They were to be like brothers. Helpers shared their homes and land. Together they were the ummah, the community.

words.d: a building where Muslims gather to pray
the Muslims who moved from Mecca to Medina
the people of Medina who helped and took in the Muslims from Mecca

look.title: Two Families, One House
look.text: Sa'd is a farmer in Medina with date palms and a house. Abd al-Rahman arrived from Mecca with nothing. Tradition says Sa'd offered him half of everything. Abd al-Rahman thanked him and said: just show me the way to the market. He started trading and soon earned his own living.
look.prompt: Both men acted well. What did each one do right? What might you do in each role?

check.q: What was the first mosque in Medina made of?
check.why: The first mosque was simple: mud-brick walls and a roof of palm branches.

check.q: Who were the Ansar?
choices: The Muslims who came from Mecca
The people of Medina who helped the newcomers
check.why: Ansar means helpers. They were the people of Medina who took in the Muslims from Mecca.

check.q: What did the Muhajirun and Ansar together form?
check.why: Muslim tradition says the two groups became one community, the ummah.

lessons.title: An Agreement for the City
lessons.mainIdea: Tradition says Muhammad made a written agreement with the tribes of Medina, Muslim and Jewish, to keep peace and defend the city together.
reading: Medina had many groups: the Muslims from Mecca, the helpers, people who had not become Muslims, and several Jewish tribes. Tradition says Muhammad made a written *agreement* with them. Later writers called it the Constitution of Medina. Historians think it is very old, though its exact words are debated.

The agreement said the groups of Medina were one community for defense. If an enemy attacked the city, all would defend it together. Each group kept its own faith. In simple words it said: the Jews have their religion, and the Muslims have theirs. Fights were to be brought to Muhammad to settle.

The peace did not last with every group. Over the next years, tradition says, three Jewish tribes and the Muslims fell out, one after another. Two tribes were made to leave the city. After a great battle in 627, the third was punished very harshly, and many of its men were killed. Historians study these events with care. They are a hard part of the story, and Muslims and scholars discuss them today.

words.d: a deal that two or more groups promise to keep
a group of people who live together and share rules or beliefs

look.title: Rules for a Shared City
look.text: Imagine a town where four different groups live. Two of them used to fight each other. A new leader asks each group to sign one paper. It says: we will all defend the town together, each group keeps its own religion, and if two groups argue, they bring it to the leader instead of fighting.
look.prompt: Which of these rules do you think was hardest to keep? Why?

check.q: What did the agreement of Medina say about religion?
choices: Each group kept its own faith
check.why: The agreement said the Jews have their religion and the Muslims have theirs.

check.q: What did all the groups promise to do together?
check.why: The groups of Medina agreed to defend the city together as one community.

check.q: How does this course talk about the falling-out with the Jewish tribes?
choices: It tells it briefly and factually, as a hard part of the story
check.why: We tell these events factually and briefly, and note that historians and Muslims discuss them.

lessons.title: Turning Toward Mecca
lessons.mainIdea: In Medina, Muslims believe, a verse told them to face the Kaaba in Mecca when they pray, instead of Jerusalem.
reading: Muslims face one direction when they pray. That direction is called the *qibla*. In Medina, tradition says, Muslims at first faced north, toward Jerusalem. Jews in Medina also prayed toward Jerusalem. For over a year, the two groups faced the same way.

Then, in about 624, Muslims believe a new verse came. It is in Surah 2, ayah 144. In simple words it says: turn your face toward the holy mosque in Mecca. Tradition says it came in the middle of a prayer. The people turned around while praying. A mosque in Medina is still called the Mosque of the Two Qiblas.

From then on, Muslims everywhere have faced the Kaaba. In Chicago, that means facing a little north of east, over the curve of the earth. Muslims read the change as a sign that their community had its own path. It also tied every prayer to the city they had left.

words.d: the direction Muslims face when they pray, toward the Kaaba in Mecca
one verse of the Qur'an

look.title: Turn Your Face
look.text: In simple words, the ayah says: We see you turning your face toward the sky. So We will surely turn you toward a qibla that will please you. Turn your face toward the holy mosque. And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it.
look.cite: Qur'an 2:144 (Al-Baqarah), paraphrased from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: Why might facing the same place, wherever you are, matter to a community that is spread out?

check.q: What is the qibla?
choices: The direction Muslims face to pray
check.why: The qibla is the direction of prayer. Since about 624 it has been the Kaaba in Mecca.

check.q: Before the change, which way did Muslims in Medina face?
check.why: At first the Muslims in Medina prayed toward Jerusalem, as the Jews there did.

check.q: Which surah and ayah speak of the new qibla?
check.why: Surah 2, Al-Baqarah, ayah 144 tells Muslims to turn toward the holy mosque.

lessons.title: Rules for a Community
lessons.mainIdea: Many Medinan verses give rules for daily life, like fasting in Ramadan and giving to the poor, because the Muslims now had a city to run.
reading: In Mecca, the surahs were short and mostly about God and the Last Day. In Medina, Muslims say, longer surahs came. They gave rules. A *rule* says what people must do. Now the Muslims were not a small group hiding from Quraysh. They were a town. A town needs rules about food, money, family and fairness.

One rule was *fasting*. Surah 2, ayah 183, says that fasting was set for the believers, as it was for people before them. Muslims fast in the month of Ramadan. They do not eat or drink from dawn to sunset. Tradition says this rule came in Medina, in the second year after the hijra.

Other verses told Muslims to give a share of their wealth to the poor. This is called *zakat*. Verses gave rules about marriage, about debts and about being honest in trade. Scholars call these the Medinan surahs. In this course you will read some of them closely in later grades.

words.d: something a group agrees people must do or must not do
going without food and drink for a set time, as Muslims do in daytime during Ramadan
the share of wealth that Muslims give to the poor each year

look.title: Fasting Is Set for You
look.text: In simple words, the ayah says: You who believe, fasting is set for you, as it was set for those who came before you, so that you may keep away from wrong.
look.cite: Qur'an 2:183 (Al-Baqarah), paraphrased from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: The ayah says people before the Muslims also fasted. Which other groups fast? Why might the verse mention them?

check.q: Why did the Medinan surahs give more rules?
choices: Because the Muslims now had a town to run
Because the Meccan surahs were lost
Because the king of Abyssinia wanted them
check.why: In Medina the Muslims were a community with a city, so verses came about daily life.

check.q: What is zakat?
choices: A share of wealth given to the poor
check.why: Zakat is the share of wealth Muslims give to the poor each year.

check.q: Which ayah sets fasting for the believers?
check.why: Surah 2, ayah 183, says fasting is set for the believers, as for those before them.

lessons.title: Badr and Uhud
lessons.mainIdea: In 624 the Muslims won a small battle at Badr, and in 625 they were hurt badly at Uhud; the Qur'an speaks about both.
reading: Quraysh and the Muslims were still enemies. In 624, tradition says, the Muslims went out to stop a rich Quraysh caravan. Quraysh sent an army to protect it. The two sides met at a well called *Badr*. The Muslims had about 300 men. Quraysh had about 1,000.

The Muslims won. Several leaders of Quraysh were killed. Muslims believe angels helped them, and Surah 8 speaks of the day. Tradition says Bilal saw his old owner among the enemy. The battle made the Muslims stronger and gave them hope.

The next year, 625, Quraysh came back with a bigger army. The sides met near a hill called *Uhud*, close to Medina. This time the Muslims were badly hurt. Muhammad's uncle Hamza was killed. Muhammad himself was wounded. Surah 3 talks about the loss and asks the believers to learn from it.

words.d: a well between Mecca and Medina where the Muslims won a battle in 624
a hill near Medina where the Muslims were badly hurt in a battle in 625

look.title: The Medina Years in Order
look.cite: Dates from Muslim tradition (the sira) and standard histories
look.prompt: How many years passed between the hijra and the return to Mecca? What happened in between?

check.q: What happened at Badr in 624?
choices: A smaller Muslim force beat a Quraysh army
The Kaaba was cleared of idols
check.why: At Badr the Muslims, about 300 men, beat an army of about 1,000 from Quraysh.

check.q: What happened at Uhud in 625?
choices: The Muslims were badly hurt and Hamza was killed
check.why: At Uhud the Muslims suffered a hard loss. Muhammad's uncle Hamza died there.

check.q: Which surah speaks about the day of Badr?
check.why: Surah 8, Al-Anfal, talks about the battle of Badr.

lessons.title: The Trench and the Treaty
lessons.mainIdea: The Muslims dug a trench to save Medina in 627, and in 628 they made a peace treaty with Quraysh at Hudaybiyyah.
reading: In 627, Quraysh and their allies came with a very large army. Tradition says a Persian Muslim named Salman had an idea. Dig a *trench*, a deep ditch, across the open side of Medina. Horses could not cross it. The army waited for weeks, then went home. Muslims call this the Battle of the Trench.

The next year, in 628, Muhammad set out for Mecca with many Muslims. They wanted to visit the Kaaba, not to fight. Quraysh stopped them at a place called *Hudaybiyyah*. After long talks, the two sides signed a *treaty*. A treaty is a written peace deal.

The treaty said there would be no fighting for ten years. The Muslims would go home now and come back to visit the Kaaba the next year. Some Muslims were upset. It felt like giving in. But tradition says Muhammad accepted it, and Surah 48 calls it a clear victory. Peace let the message spread.

words.d: a long, deep ditch dug in the ground
a written peace agreement between two sides
the place near Mecca where Muslims and Quraysh signed a peace treaty in 628

look.title: Is This a Victory?
look.text: Two Muslims walk home from Hudaybiyyah. One says: We came all this way and did not even see the Kaaba. Quraysh got what they wanted. This is a loss. The other says: For ten years no one will attack us. We can travel, trade and talk to anyone. More people will hear the message. This is a win.
look.prompt: Which friend do you agree with, and why? What does Surah 48 suggest?

check.q: What idea saved Medina in 627?
choices: Asking the Persian king for help
Digging a trench that horses could not cross
check.why: Tradition credits Salman with the plan to dig a trench across the open side of the city.

check.q: What is a treaty?
check.why: A treaty is a written peace deal between two sides, like the one at Hudaybiyyah.

check.q: What did the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah say?
choices: No fighting for ten years, and Muslims could visit the Kaaba the next year
check.why: The treaty set ten years of peace and let the Muslims come back the next year to visit the Kaaba.

lessons.title: Back to Mecca
lessons.mainIdea: In 630 Muhammad returned to Mecca with a large group, the city gave in almost without a fight, and the idols were taken out of the Kaaba.
reading: The peace did not last ten years. In 630, tradition says, allies of Quraysh attacked allies of the Muslims. This broke the treaty. Muhammad gathered a very large group, about 10,000 people, and marched to Mecca. Quraysh saw they could not win.

Most of Mecca gave in without a fight. Tradition says Muhammad forgave nearly everyone, even old enemies. He then went to the Kaaba. Muslims say he broke the idols inside it and had them carried out. He said the Kaaba was now for the one God only, as Ibrahim had built it.

Bilal climbed to the top of the Kaaba and gave the call to prayer. Tradition says some of Quraysh's old leaders became Muslims that day. Many tribes across Arabia then joined the Muslims. Within two years, Muslims say, most of Arabia had accepted the message.

words.d: to stop being angry at someone for what they did, and not punish them
taking control of a place; Muslims call the return to Mecca the Conquest of Mecca

look.title: Picture the Kaaba That Day
look.text: Picture the square building in the middle of Mecca. A huge crowd stands around it. Men carry stone statues out through the door and set them down in the dust. A tall man climbs up onto the roof of the building and calls out over the crowd. Old enemies stand in the crowd, waiting to hear what will happen to them.
look.prompt: Why do you think Muslim tradition remembers that Muhammad forgave his old enemies that day?

check.q: How did Mecca give in, in 630?
check.why: Tradition says the city gave in almost without fighting, and most people were forgiven.

check.q: What happened to the idols in the Kaaba?
choices: They were kept in a corner
They were broken and taken out
check.why: Muslims say Muhammad had the idols broken and removed, so the Kaaba was for one God.

check.q: Who gave the call to prayer from the top of the Kaaba?
check.why: Tradition says Bilal climbed the Kaaba and called the Muslims to prayer.

sections.title: The Last Years and the Book

lessons.title: The Farewell Sermon
lessons.mainIdea: On his last pilgrimage in 632, tradition says, Muhammad gave a speech about fairness and equality that Muslims still quote.
reading: In 632, Muhammad made a *pilgrimage* to Mecca. A pilgrimage is a holy trip. Muslims call this one the Farewell Pilgrimage, because it was his last. Tradition says he spoke to a huge crowd on a plain near Mecca. Muslims call the speech the Farewell Sermon.

Tradition reports his words this way. He said every Muslim is a brother to every other Muslim. He said an Arab is not better than a non-Arab, and a non-Arab is not better than an Arab. He said no one is better because of skin color. Only good deeds make a person better.

He told the crowd to treat women well. He told them to be fair about money and debts. He asked if he had passed on the message. The crowd said yes. Muslims connect this speech to Surah 49, ayah 13. That ayah says God made nations and tribes so people could know one another. The exact words come from later reports, so versions differ a little.

words.d: a trip to a holy place; the Muslim pilgrimage to Mecca is called hajj
a speech about faith and how to live, given to a gathered crowd
the idea that people have the same worth and deserve the same fair treatment

look.title: Nations and Tribes
look.text: In simple words, the ayah says: People, We made you from a male and a female. We made you into nations and tribes so that you could get to know one another. The best of you, in God's sight, is the one who acts best. God knows everything.
look.cite: Qur'an 49:13 (Al-Hujurat), paraphrased from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: What does this ayah say makes one person better than another? What does it say does not?

check.q: What is a pilgrimage?
choices: A trip to a holy place
check.why: A pilgrimage is a holy trip. Muhammad's last one, in 632, is called the Farewell Pilgrimage.

check.q: According to the Farewell Sermon, what makes one person better than another?
check.why: Tradition says the sermon taught that only good deeds, not tribe or color, make a person better.

check.q: Which ayah do Muslims connect to the sermon's idea of equality?
check.why: Surah 49:13 says God made people into nations and tribes so they could know one another.

lessons.title: The Prophet Dies
lessons.mainIdea: Muhammad died in Medina in 632; Muslims believe the Qur'an was complete, and Abu Bakr became the first leader after him.
reading: A few months after the pilgrimage, Muhammad became ill. He died in Medina in the year 632. Tradition says he was about 63. He was buried in his wife Aisha's room, next to the mosque. Today that spot is inside the Prophet's Mosque, under a green dome.

Many Muslims could not believe he was gone. Tradition says Abu Bakr stood up and spoke. He said: whoever worshipped Muhammad, know that Muhammad has died. Whoever worships God, know that God lives and does not die. Then he read an ayah, 3:144, which says Muhammad is only a messenger, and messengers before him have died.

The Muslims chose Abu Bakr as their leader. His title was *caliph*, which means "one who comes after." Not all Muslims agreed on who should lead. Shia Muslims believe Ali should have led first. This is one root of the difference between Sunni and Shia Muslims today. Muslims believe no new revelation came after Muhammad.

words.d: the leader of the Muslim community after Muhammad; the word means one who comes after
the two largest groups of Muslims, who differ on who should have led after Muhammad

look.title: Only a Messenger
look.text: In simple words, the ayah says: Muhammad is only a messenger. Messengers have passed away before him. If he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels? Whoever turns back will not hurt God at all. And God will reward the thankful.
look.cite: Qur'an 3:144 (Al 'Imran), paraphrased from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: Why might Abu Bakr have chosen this ayah to read on the day Muhammad died?

check.q: Where did Muhammad die, and in what year?
check.why: Muhammad died in Medina in 632, about ten years after the hijra.

check.q: What does the word caliph mean?
check.why: Caliph means one who comes after, or successor. Abu Bakr was the first.

check.q: What do Shia Muslims believe about the first leader after Muhammad?
choices: Abu Bakr was the right choice
check.why: Shia Muslims believe Ali, Muhammad's cousin, should have been the first leader.

lessons.title: Gathering the Book
lessons.mainIdea: Muslim tradition says the Qur'an was written down in one book after Muhammad's death, first under Abu Bakr and then in a standard copy under Uthman.
reading: During Muhammad's life, the Qur'an lived mostly in people's memory. Many Muslims knew it by heart. Some parts were also written down by a *scribe* on bones, leather, palm stalks and flat stones. Tradition names Zayd ibn Thabit as one of the scribes who wrote the words down as they came.

In a battle soon after Muhammad died, many of the men who knew the Qur'an by heart were killed. Tradition says Umar worried the book could be lost. Abu Bakr asked Zayd to gather every part. Zayd collected the written pieces and checked them against what people had memorized. He made one set of pages.

About twenty years later, in about 650, Muslims had spread to many lands. People read some words a little differently. The third caliph, *Uthman*, asked Zayd and others to make one standard copy. Copies were sent to the main cities. Muslims believe the Qur'an read today is the same text. Scholars study very old copies to learn how it was written.

words.d: a person whose job is to write things down by hand
the third caliph, who tradition says had a standard copy of the Qur'an made in about 650
to learn something so well that you can say it without looking

look.title: Memory and Ink
look.text: Two ways of keeping a text safe. Way one: many people learn it by heart and recite it every day, so one mistake gets caught by the others. Way two: it is written down and copied with care, so it does not depend on anyone's memory. Muslim tradition says the Qur'an was kept both ways.
look.prompt: What could go wrong with each way alone? Why might using both be safer?

check.q: Who does tradition say gathered the Qur'an into one set of pages under Abu Bakr?
check.why: Zayd ibn Thabit, a scribe, collected the written pieces and checked them against memory.

check.q: Why did Abu Bakr want the Qur'an gathered?
choices: Many who knew it by heart had died in battle
The king of Persia asked for it
check.why: After a battle killed many memorizers, Umar and Abu Bakr feared the text could be lost.

check.q: What did Uthman do in about 650?
choices: Had a standard copy made and sent to the main cities
check.why: Uthman, the third caliph, had one standard copy made and sent to major cities.

review.q: Why do Muslims count years from 622?
choices: The Kaaba was built that year
The hijra to Medina happened that year
The Qur'an was finished that year
review.why: The Hijri calendar starts at the hijra, the move from Mecca to Medina in 622.
The town was called Yathrib. People renamed it the City of the Prophet, Medina.

review.q: What did the agreement of Medina say about the Jewish tribes?
choices: They kept their religion and shared in defending the city
They had to leave at once
review.why: The agreement said each group kept its faith and all would defend the city together.

review.q: Put these in order: Uhud, Badr, the Trench.
review.why: Badr was in 624, Uhud in 625, and the Trench in 627.

review.q: What did the treaty of Hudaybiyyah bring?
choices: Ten years of peace with Quraysh
review.why: The 628 treaty set peace for ten years. Surah 48 calls it a clear victory.

review.q: What happened at the Kaaba in 630?
choices: It was turned into a mosque for many gods
review.why: When Mecca gave in, Muhammad had the idols removed from the Kaaba.

review.q: What did the Farewell Sermon teach about Arabs and non-Arabs?
choices: Neither is better than the other; only deeds count
review.why: Tradition says the sermon taught that no one is better by tribe or color, only by good deeds.

review.q: As Muslim tradition tells it, when was the Qur'an gathered into one book?
choices: After Muhammad's death, under Abu Bakr and then Uthman
review.why: Tradition says Abu Bakr had it gathered, and Uthman made a standard copy in about 650.
